evidence.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (EUR-Lex), Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
evidence.supportedAssertion: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) applies from 11 December 2027, except the reporting obligations concerning actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, which apply from 11 September 2026, and the provisions on notification of conformity assessment bodies, which apply from 11 June 2026 (recital 126). Article 6 makes products whose core functionality is not listed in Annex III default products with digital elements; Article 7 makes products whose core functionality is listed in Annex III 'important products with digital elements' (classes I and II) subject to the stricter conformity assessment of Article 32(2) and (3); Article 8 allows delegated acts to require a European cybersecurity certification for 'critical products with digital elements' listed in Annex IV. Article 7(4) required the Commission to adopt an implementing act specifying the technical descriptions of the Annex III and Annex IV categories by 11 December 2025.
evidence.limitations: The EUR-Lex HTML retrieval was truncated before Article 71 and before Annex I–VIII, so the final Article 71 wording, the Annex III/IV category lists and the Annex I essential-requirement text were NOT retrieved in this session. The application dates above are quoted from recital 126 of the retrieved text. Whether any MAREA product is default, 'important' (class I or II) or 'critical' is NOT established by this record and depends on the implementing act's technical descriptions, which were not retrieved here.

evidence.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (EUR-Lex), Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
evidence.supportedAssertion: Article 13 of the CRA requires manufacturers to design, develop and produce products in accordance with the essential cybersecurity requirements of Annex I Part I; to document a cybersecurity risk assessment updated during the support period (13(3)); to exercise due diligence over third-party components (13(5)); to report component vulnerabilities upstream and share fixes (13(6)); to determine a support period reflecting expected use that is at least five years (13(8)); to have policies and procedures including coordinated vulnerability disclosure policies (13(8)); to keep each security update available for at least 10 years or the remainder of the support period, whichever is longer (13(9)); to draw up technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity and affix CE marking after conformity assessment (13(12)); to keep documentation for at least 10 years or the support period (13(13)); to indicate a type/batch/serial number (13(15)); to designate a single point of contact for users and vulnerability reporting (13(17)); to provide user information and instructions (13(18)); to specify the end date of the support period, at least month and year, at the time of purchase (13(19)); to take corrective measures, withdraw or recall a non-conforming product (13(21)); to inform authorities and users before ceasing operations (13(23)); and to provide a software bill of materials as referred to in Annex I Part II point (1), whose format the Commission may specify by implementing act (13(24)).
evidence.limitations: Annex I itself was not rendered by the retrieval; the obligation references to Annex I Part I points (1) and (2) and Part II points (1), (2), (5) and (8) are quoted as they appear in Article 13, but their full content is NOT verified from a fetched source. This record establishes that the obligations exist, not that MAREA satisfies any of them.

evidence.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (EUR-Lex), Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
evidence.supportedAssertion: Article 14 of the CRA requires a manufacturer to notify any actively exploited vulnerability in a product with digital elements, and any severe incident having an impact on the security of the product, simultaneously to the CSIRT designated as coordinator and to ENISA through the single reporting platform: an early warning without undue delay and within 24 hours; a vulnerability or incident notification within 72 hours; a final report for a vulnerability no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available, and for an incident within one month after the 72-hour notification. Article 14(5) defines a severe incident as one that negatively affects or is capable of negatively affecting the product's ability to protect availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of sensitive or important data or functions, or that has led or could lead to the introduction or execution of malicious code. Article 14(8) requires the manufacturer to inform impacted users of the vulnerability or incident and of mitigation measures. Article 15 provides for voluntary reporting.
evidence.limitations: Article 16 (the single reporting platform procedure) and the delegated/implementing acts on delaying dissemination were not retrieved. The reporting process is therefore known only from Article 14 and Article 15 text; no ENISA platform process, account or registration was accessed or tested.

evidence.supportedAssertion: ENISA operates the Single Reporting Platform (SRP) established for the Cyber Resilience Act, through which manufacturers report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents in products with digital elements once, to a designated coordinator CSIRT and ENISA; ENISA states that the CRA Article 14 reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026. ENISA also operates the European Vulnerability Database (EUVD), is a CVE Numbering Authority and CVE Root, publishes the EU KEV catalogue, and supports coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) with guidance and good-practice material for Member States.
evidence.limitations: Agency service overview page, not the legal text and not a reporting procedure specification. It does not state form fields, account prerequisites or national coordinator details for Spain/Portugal. No ENISA service was registered for or tested by MAREA.

evidence.supportedAssertion: The MicroPython repository licence file states the MIT licence (copyright 2013-2026 Damien P. George) for the repository unless specified otherwise, and lists per-directory third-party components: the rp2 port files mutex_extra.c and clocks_extra.c under BSD-3-clause, pico-sdk under BSD-3-clause, lwip, littlefs, axtls, re15, nrfx, nxp_driver, open-amp and stm32lib under BSD-3-clause, tinyusb and wiznet5k under MIT, uzlib under Zlib, the logo under OFL-1.1, and tools/dfu.py under LGPL-3.0-only; it notes that (L)GPL-licensed code listed is used only during the build process and is not part of the compiled source code.

The exact notices that must ship with a programmed board depend on the pinned MicroPython revision, the port and every enabled module; that mapping was NOT produced in this session, and no board or firmware image exists.

evidence.supportedAssertion: NXP's EdgeLock SE050 page describes a Plug and Trust secure-element family that is Common Criteria EAL 6+ certified up to OS level, is part of the EdgeLock Assurance programme, and is stated to be available for a minimum of 10 years (15 years for designated automotive, telecom and medical products). The page names the EdgeLock 2GO provisioning/onboarding service and Plug & Trust middleware packages for MCU/MPU integration, and states that some software downloads require an account.
evidence.limitations: Marketing product-family page, not a datasheet, security target, price list, lifecycle certificate or MOQ statement. No interface, supply, temperature or key-slot detail was rendered. The part was NOT registered in the MC-11 component register and no alternative selection was made. Third-party CC certificate number and scope were not retrieved.

evidence.supportedAssertion: ST's STSAFE-A120 product page describes a secure authentication companion device: Common Criteria EAL5+ AVA_VAN.5 with ALC_DVS.2; unique ID; ECDSA/EdDSA signature generation and verification and ECDH; AES-128/256 with CCM, GCM, CMAC and HKDF; SHA-2/SHA-3; a NIST SP 800-90B compliant RNG; 16 Kbytes of configurable nonvolatile memory with 25 years data retention at 25 degrees C and 500 000 erase/write cycles; 2.7-5.5 V supply; -40 to +105 degrees C; I2C up to 400 kbps; SO8N/UFDFPN packages. The page lists a signature-verification service for secure boot and firmware upgrade, host pairing and secure channel, TLS 1.2/1.3 handshake, and customer-specific secrets loaded at ST manufacturing as a personalization service. The product status is shown as active, with availability until 01/2035.
evidence.limitations: Marketing product page, not a datasheet or security target. Personalization-service contract terms, key-management responsibility split, SDK/ middleware licence terms and per-unit provisioning cost were NOT retrieved. The part was NOT registered in the MC-11 component register and is not a selection.

evidence.supportedAssertion: Microchip's ATECC608B page states the device status as 'Not Recommended for new designs'. It describes a secure element with ECC-P256 (ECDH and ECDSA), SHA-256/HMAC and AES-128-GCM, protected storage for up to 16 keys, certificates or data, two high-endurance monotonic counters, a guaranteed unique 72-bit serial number, a NIST SP 800-90 A/B/C random number generator, a 1.8-5.5 V IO / 2.0-5.5 V supply range, <150 nA sleep current, operating temperature up to 100 degrees C, I2C up to 1 MHz or single-wire interface, and secure-boot support through full ECDSA code-signature validation with optional stored digest/signature. The page names Trust&GO (pre-provisioned), TrustFLEX (pre-configured) and TrustCUSTOM variants.
evidence.limitations: Marketing product page, not a datasheet, security target or lifecycle PCN. 'Guaranteed unique 72-bit serial number' is the manufacturer's page wording, quoted as a manufacturer statement and not independently verified. NRND is the material finding already recorded by the sourcing workstream (CMP-SEC-01/CMP-SEC-02); alternatives were not evaluated, so no replacement part is proposed here.

evidence.supportedAssertion: Toradex documents production programming of secure boot for Torizon OS based modules: secure boot is configured by programming one-time-programmable e-fuses with the public key information of the signing PKI tree (8 fuse values for HAB, 16 for AHAB) and then, as the last step, setting a closing fuse; once the closing fuse is blown the SoC does not load an image not signed with the correct PKI tree and the operation cannot be reversed. Automatic fusing on first boot requires a Torizon OS image of at least version 7.2.0 with at least the Basic Chain of Trust configured and TorizonCore Builder of at least version 3.13.0 (3.17.0 for the build-command approach). The documented fusing logic avoids closing the device if fuse programming errors or HAB/AHAB events are reported. In-field fusing uses Torizon Cloud and requires a commercial licence for the Torizon Cloud account.
evidence.limitations: Vendor documentation for one SOM family and one OS/BSP path (Torizon OS and Yocto). It documents the mechanism and its irreversibility, not a MAREA design, key hierarchy, HSM choice, manufacturing station or test. It does not state which modules support which fuse-programming options; that matrix is referenced but was not retrieved. No MAREA image, PKI tree or product exists.

evidence.supportedAssertion: MCUboot documentation describes a secure bootloader for 32-bit microcontrollers that defines a common bootloader and flash layout on MCU systems, enables signed-image boot and software upgrade, provides an image signing tool (imgtool) and a serial recovery protocol (MCUmgr) for recovery of a device without a working application.
evidence.limitations: Open-source project documentation; the licence of the MCUboot project itself was NOT retrieved in this session and is not asserted. No MCU target, boot-time measurement, rollback test or compatibility assessment was performed. MCUboot is named as a candidate mechanism only.

evidence.supportedAssertion: RAUC documentation describes a lightweight embedded-Linux update client with fail-safe and atomic updates ('an update may be interrupted at any point without breaking the running system'), cryptographic signing and verification of update bundles using OpenSSL with X.509 certificates, support for keys and certificates on PKCS#11 tokens (HSMs), marking boots as successful or failed, symmetric A/B root-filesystem or asymmetric recovery/normal layouts, a bootloader interface, and eMMC boot-partition/ext4/UBI/UBIFS/raw-NAND/raw-NOR storage support. It states that RAUC is not a deployment server and does not replace the bootloader.
evidence.limitations: Open-source project documentation; the RAUC licence was NOT retrieved and is not asserted. It does not cover MCU-class targets. No integration, bundle, key ceremony, A/B test, power-loss test or measured boot time exists. RAUC is a candidate mechanism only.

evidence.publisher: U-Boot project (board documentation authored by a Toradex engineer)
evidence.supportedAssertion: The upstream U-Boot board document for the Toradex Verdin i.MX8M Plus states the build and boot flow: build the ARM Trusted Firmware (TF-A), obtain the NXP DDR firmware from the firmware-imx package (a vendor binary distribution) and copy the lpddr4 training binaries, build U-Boot, flash to eMMC; ATF, U-Boot proper and the device tree are packed into a FIT image loaded and parsed by SPL, with the boot sequence SPL -> ATF (TF-A) -> U-Boot proper and the example log showing the SoC BootROM handing over to SPL. The file is marked SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later.
evidence.limitations: Upstream community/vendor-authored board document, not a MAREA BSP. It establishes that the documented i.MX8M Plus boot flow depends on vendor TF-A and a vendor DDR-firmware binary blob, but the exact BSP revision, blob licence terms, redistribution conditions and notice obligations were NOT retrieved. The document's own GPL-2.0-or-later SPDX tag applies to the document, not to MAREA code.
